title: Query trace: clause-by-clause dry run (hr / shop)

blocks.md: SQL gives you no step button — you write the whole query or nothing. A **query-trace** runs it clause by clause and shows the intermediate table after each step: hit **Run trace** to boot PostgreSQL, then step with **Prev / Next** (or toggle **Show all**). Every row a clause eliminated stays in the table struck through, so a filter's victims — and a join trap's silent losses — are impossible to miss.

blocks.title: WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING: who earns what per department

stages.label: FROM
stages.note: Logical step 1 — **FROM** decides which rows every later clause gets to see: 21 employees, nothing filtered or grouped yet.

stages.label: WHERE
stages.sql:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, e.dept_id, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary >= 80000
ORDER BY e.emp_id;
stages.note: **WHERE** runs before any grouping: rows failing the predicate never reach the aggregator — 7 employees (salary below 80000) drop right here.

stages.label: GROUP BY
stages.sql:
SELECT e.dept_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount, MAX(e.salary) AS top_salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary >= 80000
GROUP BY e.dept_id
ORDER BY e.dept_id;
stages.note: **GROUP BY** collapses the 14 survivors into one row per department. Individual names are gone — COUNT/MAX are computed inside each group. The columns changed, so there is nothing row-for-row to diff against the last stage.

stages.label: HAVING
stages.sql:
SELECT e.dept_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount, MAX(e.salary) AS top_salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary >= 80000
GROUP BY e.dept_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY e.dept_id;
stages.note: **HAVING** filters the *groups* after they already exist: Executive and HR each kept only one ≥80k earner, so both groups are removed. WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

stages.label: SELECT
stages.sql:
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(*) AS headcount, MAX(e.salary) AS top_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary >= 80000
GROUP BY d.dept_name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
stages.note: The SELECT list swaps `dept_id` for the department's name, so the join to `departments` happens before grouping. No ORDER BY here — 4 rows, but their order is the engine's choice, not a promise.

stages.label: ORDER BY
stages.sql:
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(*) AS headcount, MAX(e.salary) AS top_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary >= 80000
GROUP BY d.dept_name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY d.dept_name;
stages.note: **ORDER BY** is the only clause that changes *no rows* — same 4 rows, sorted by name. Here stage 5 returned them in that order anyway (the engine used the unique index on `dept_name`): luck, not a guarantee. Never rely on a stage's order unless ORDER BY says so.

blocks.title: LEFT JOIN trap: WHERE on the right table kills the NULL rows

stages.label: FROM · LEFT JOIN
stages.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;
stages.note: 30 orders + 1 filler row = **31 rows**: every customer survives the LEFT JOIN, and Arnav Bose (customer 11, never ordered) keeps his row with `order_id` NULL.

stages.label: WHERE on the right table (the trap)
stages.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'cancelled'
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;
stages.note: The classic trap: `WHERE o.status = ...` is evaluated *after* the join, and NULL fails every comparison — so the LEFT JOIN quietly behaves like an INNER JOIN. **29 rows vanish**, including Arnav's NULL filler row; only the 2 cancelled orders survive. Filtering the left table would have been harmless; filtering the right one re-decides the join.

stages.label: Fix: filter before joining
stages.note: Push the predicate **into a derived table** so only cancelled orders ever meet the join. Now 12 rows come back: 2 cancelled orders + 10 NULL-filled customers — unmatched customers no longer depend on what the WHERE clause thinks of NULL.
